text: Two reels survive and not one intertitle, so what remains of Marion E. Wong's film has to be read off faces, gestures and rooms. She made it in 1916: the oldest Chinese-American film anyone has found, and among the earliest American silent features directed by a woman. A trade notice from 1917 described the curse of a Chinese god pursuing his people because of the influence of western civilization, which is as close to a plot as the surviving footage will allow, and around it runs the plainer matter of what assimilation costs the people performing it. No distributor would buy a Chinese-American picture that declined the usual stereotypes. It lost money, played twice more, and went quiet for eighty-seven years. Rediscovered in 2004, thirty-five minutes long, half a story — and the intent still legible in every surviving frame.

Dorothy's week is organized by the welfare office: the trip there, the wait, the same questions asked again. Haile Gerima built Bush Mama around that rhythm rather than around incident — errands, corridors, a neighborhood where work is scarce and rent is not. Her husband T.C. came home from Vietnam expecting the welcome he had been promised and was arrested instead for a crime that was not his, which leaves Dorothy answering to two bureaucracies at once: one that pays her too little, one that has taken him. Radicalization here is not an argument won on a page. It is arithmetic that stops balancing. The film extends her patience no credit as virtue; it watches the patience wear through, hour by ordinary hour, over ninety-seven minutes in which the most political act on screen is keeping an appointment.

Filed under drama, which is the least useful fact on its record. Sidney Peterson spends eighteen minutes removing the two supports a viewer never notices using: a sense of where things are, and a sense of when. Neither eye nor ear is given a fixed reference; distance and duration are offered only in relation to each other, and the relation keeps moving. That disorientation is not decoration applied to a story. It is the subject. Made in the United States in 1949, at a remove from the continuity habits of the studios, the film treats perception as something to be argued with rather than served. Eighteen minutes is the right measure for it — long enough for the floor to go out, short enough that the method never hardens into a system.

A town called Torpedo wants its famous son back for Frontier Days, and it has a ceremonial badge waiting for him. Honorary sheriff is a title designed to mean nothing, which in a 1940 western amounts to a guarantee that it will shortly have to mean something. Arizona, eighty-four minutes, and the interest lies less in frontier danger than in what a hometown does with a man who left and became known elsewhere: the parade, the pageantry, the civic pride with a printed schedule. Joseph Santley keeps the register light and unhurried. Trouble arrives through the door all that self-congratulation leaves standing open. Gene is welcomed as a symbol and then needed as a person, and the distance between those two jobs is what the film actually attends to.

The subject is what a respectable household in 1945 will not say out loud, and what becomes of the daughter left to find out by experiment. She is a teenager from a traditional family; the man is a pilot; the evening is brief and its consequences are not. Ninety-seven minutes is generous for a cautionary tale, and the generosity is the tell — there is room here for the transgression and the lecture both, and no intention of skipping either. William Beaudine works by escalation rather than nuance, which is what this material asks for. The National Film Registry keeps it now, a decision about the shape of American squeamishness more than about craft. The concern on offer is also merchandise, and the film is unembarrassed by the trade.

Evening clothes, a song, and jokes delivered as though they had been assigned rather than chosen. Shaw and Lee were a vaudeville team, and these nine minutes are their act carried over intact: patter, tunes, and a flat refusal to sell any of it. The deadpan is the entire method. The camera has no ideas about them, which is the correct decision, because what is being kept here is timing — including the pauses, which a printed joke cannot hold and which are most of the comedy. 1928, one reel, two men who behave as if amusing anyone would be beneath them. The act came off a stage and the film makes no attempt to disguise the fact. Material like this dates fast and delivery like this does not; the routine is a museum piece and the silences between its lines are still working.

A ship carrying prospectors north catches fire, and in the confusion a mother and her small daughter lose each other. What follows is not a rescue but a long detour: the girl grows up in the goldfields in the care of two men, 'Horseshoe' Riley and Bob Dexter, who have no business raising a child and do it anyway. Eighty-seven minutes from 1924, and the balance is odd in a useful way — half adventure, with ice and distance and the traffic of people chasing a strike, half a domestic arrangement improvised by men whose trade is luck. Melodrama of this vintage usually treats a missing mother as a debt the plot must repay. The better part of this one is the interval before any repayment, the years in which the substitute household is simply the household.

Sunday is the only day they have, and Sunday is when everything that might help them is closed. The couple in Lee Man-hee's film are unmarried and short of money; she is pregnant and does not believe the world they live in is fit to receive a child; he sets out to borrow the cost of the delivery from friends. Seventy-four minutes, made in South Korea in 1968, and it moves the way an empty afternoon moves — walking, sitting, one more address to try. The pressure is never staged as crisis. It is arithmetic: the fare, the sum, the exact wording needed to ask a friend for it. KOFA keeps the film among its hundred, and the reason is audible in the pacing rather than the plot — a weekly meeting that has quietly become the entire shape of two lives.

The sheriff is not entirely incorruptible, and that one qualification keeps the story from turning into a sermon. Jim Stokes robs a stage, takes a bullet getting clear, and recovers in a settler's house, where the daughter gives him a reason to want to be someone else. Eighty minutes, 1914, and the length goes to the middle of the story rather than the chase — reform as an arrangement to be negotiated, not a change of heart between reels. Reginald Barker builds his frontier out of terms and conditions: a wound, a debt, a proposition put by a lawman who has worked out what the situation is worth to him. The romance sets the price. The law adjusts it. For a genre that runs on clean lines, a crooked one turns out to be the more interesting instrument.

Three brothers who agree on almost nothing keep meeting in the middle of a song. Dave wants a garage and a wife; Mike wants to stay a boy a while longer; Joe wants a shortcut, which he keeps mistaking for a plan. The singing act is the one room their incompatible schemes can share, and two of the three resent being in it. Wesley Ruggles finds his comedy in that resentment rather than in gags — a household where affection and exasperation are spoken in the same tone of voice. Eighty-eight minutes, 1938, and the songs work as truce rather than production number. The National Board of Review put it among the year's ten, a mildly surprising place for a picture this domestic. Joe's latest acquisition is a racehorse, and his family does not yet know how large a bet he has laid on it.

The work is high up: painting other people's advertisements on the side of a building, several storeys above a street that never looks up. Chilsu drifts between jobs and improves his own life in the telling; Mansu, the sign painter, keeps his account shorter. What Park Kwang-su gets out of the pair in 1988 is the gap between what the two men claim and what their hands do all day, which is brushwork on a face far larger and happier than either of theirs. One hundred and nine minutes, and the register shifts without notice. When they climb onto the top of the billboard, the crowd below assembles its own explanation for two men standing where nobody stands, and being explained by strangers turns out to be a trap of its own. One of the hundred films KOFA keeps.

There is an American hidden in an Umbrian farmhouse, and above him a family performing an ordinary day so that nobody looks twice. Uncle Tigna took him in along with two others, which makes hospitality a form of exposure: every knock, every requisition, every neighbor with an opinion about the household. Luigi Zampa made the film in 1947, while all of it was still recent, and his method is to let farce and dread occupy one room — a night on which the escaped prisoner and a German soldier, both very drunk, agree that the war is over and embrace each other. For a few minutes the mistake holds. Eighty-seven minutes, and the Nastro d'Argento for its story went to a script that understands how much wartime courage is improvised by people who would rather be minding a farm.

An American photographer stayed in Warsaw while the Wehrmacht closed on the city, and ten minutes of what he exposed there became this film. Julien Bryan had come out of Pennsylvania with a camera; he left with footage of a European capital under artillery in the first weeks of a war that most of his eventual audience had heard about and not yet seen. Assembled in 1940, it belongs to the narrow period when the distance between a report and an image could still change what people believed. Its method is proximity and its authority is simply having been there. When the Librarian of Congress later called it a record of the brutality of war, the word carrying the weight was record: this is what a city looks like while it is being taken.

Ray and Esther owned a camera, and in 1939 they pointed it at Cologne, Minnesota — its streets, its work, the people they already knew by name. Fourteen minutes, no commission behind it, and the amateur footing is exactly where the value sits: nobody in frame is performing for a distributor, and the camera goes no further than the acquaintance does. What a film like this holds is local and unrepeatable — which store, which field, which faces on which morning of a year the rest of the country was measuring in other terms. Esther Dowidat is credited as director. The National Film Registry keeps it now, less for craft than for survival: a small place recorded at eye level by someone who had to go on living in it afterward.
